body:
ALBUQUERQUE – Today, the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico announced its immigration enforcement statistics. These cases are prosecuted in partnership with the El Paso Sector of the U.S. Border Patrol, along with Homeland Security Investigations El Paso, and assistance from other federal, state, and county agencies. 

In the four-week period ending October 2, 2026, the United States Attorney’s Office brought the following criminal charges in New Mexico:

  • 288 individuals were charged with Illegal Reentry After Deportation (8 U.S.C. 1326)
  • 23 individuals were charged with Alien Smuggling (8 U.S.C. 1324)
  • 232 individuals were charged with Illegal Entry (8 U.S.C. 1325)
  • 284 individuals were charged with Illegal Entry (8 U.S.C. 1325), violation of a military security regulation (50 U.S.C. 797) and Entering Military, Naval, or Coast Guard Property (18 U.S.C. 1382), arising from the newly established National Defense Area in New Mexico. 

Many of the defendants charged pursuant to 8 U.S.C. 1326 had prior criminal convictions for child molestation, drug possession, and theft, possession with intent to distribute narcotics, grand theft, and prior immigration offenses.

These cases are part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

These statistics represent prosecutions by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico only. The numbers do not include individuals apprehended by immigration enforcement officials and subjected solely to administrative process.

Under current leadership, public safety and a secure border are the top priorities for the District of New Mexico. Enhanced enforcement both at the border and in the interior of the district have yielded aliens engaged in unlawful activity or with serious criminal history, including human trafficking, sexual assault and violence against children. 

The District of New Mexico consists of 33 counties and shares 180 miles of international border with Mexico.  Assistant U.S. Attorneys from Albuquerque and Las Cruces work directly with our federal, state and local law enforcement partners to prosecute immigration-related and other federal offenses.

title: U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico Weekly Immigration and Border Crimes Report

body:
ALBUQUERQUE – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico joins the Department of Justice, the Office on Violence Against Women and communities across New Mexico in recognizing October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month and reaffirming its commitment to protecting victims, holding offenders accountable and supporting the organizations that serve survivors.

“Protecting victims of domestic violence takes coordinated work from law enforcement, prosecutors, advocates and service providers.,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “These grants strengthen that work across New Mexico, and our office will continue doing its part to protect victims and pursue offenders under federal law.”

As part of that effort, the Department of Justice recently awarded $106,581 to the New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence and $236,484 to the New Mexico Coalition of Sexual Assault Programs, Inc. The two organizations are New Mexico’s designated statewide domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions.

“Domestic violence has a devastating impact that reaches far beyond an individual survivor—it affects children, families, communities, and generations,” said MaryEllen Garcia, CEO of New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence. “During Domestic Violence Awareness Month, we honor the courage of survivors while also recognizing the extraordinary work happening every day across New Mexico. The New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence is proud to stand alongside our statewide network of domestic violence providers, whose advocates show up every day with compassion, skill, and an unwavering commitment to survivor safety, dignity, and choice. Ending domestic violence requires all of us—advocates, law enforcement, prosecutors, courts, community partners, and neighbors—working together to build communities where survivors are supported, people who cause harm are held accountable, and everyone has the opportunity to live free from violence.”

Domestic Violence Awareness Month provides an opportunity to recognize the work of victim advocates, law enforcement officers, prosecutors, healthcare professionals and community organizations responding to domestic violence throughout New Mexico. It also highlights the role friends, relatives, coworkers and neighbors can play in recognizing abuse and helping victims connect with available resources.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office works with federal, Tribal, state and local law enforcement and prosecutors to enforce federal laws applicable to domestic violence, including federal firearms laws intended to keep firearms out of the hands of certain individuals prohibited from possessing them because of domestic violence convictions or qualifying protection orders.

The Department of Justice also supports victim services through grant programs administered by the Office on Violence Against Women and the Office for Victims of Crime. OVW identifies the New Mexico Coalition Against Domestic Violence and the New Mexico Coalition of Sexual Assault Programs, Inc. as the state’s designated domestic violence and sexual assault coalitions for fiscal year 2026.

Help is available through the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) and the StrongHearts Native Helpline at 1-844-7NATIVE (762-8483). Additional resources for victims and survivors are available through the Office on Violence Against Women at justice.gov/ovw.
teaser: The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico joins the Department of Justice, the Office on Violence Against Women and communities across New Mexico in recognizing October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month and reaffirming its commitment to protecting victims, holding offenders accountable and supporting the organizations that serve survivors.
title: U.S. Attorney’s Office Marks Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Highlights Federal Funding for New Mexico Victim Services

body:
ALBUQUERQUE – A Farmington man has been charged federally in connection with the alleged sexual abuse of two minor victims.

According to court documents, on September 19, 2026, and on previous occasions, Raleigh Jackson, 34, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, engaged in sex acts with two minor victims.

Jackson is charged with two counts of aggravated sexual abuse and will remain on conditions of release pending trial which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted, Jackson faces up to life in prison. 

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicholas J. Marshall is prosecuting the case. 

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
teaser: Raleigh Jackson has been charged federally in connection with the alleged sexual abuse of two minor victims.
title: Farmington Man Charged with Sexually Abusing Two Children

ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock man has been indicted in connection with four alleged sexual assaults that occurred over a two-year period.

According to court documents, on four occasions between May 2018, and May 2020, Pierson Manycattle, 28, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, engaged in sex acts with a minor. 

Manycattle is charged with three counts of aggravated sexual abuse and one count of abusive sexual contact and will remain on conditions of release pending trial which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted, Manycattle faces up to life in prison. 

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicholas J. Marshall is prosecuting the case. 

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

body:
ALBUQUERQUE – Three men are facing federal charges for allegedly beating a man with a sledgehammer and dumbbells, leaving him with life-threatening injuries.

According to court documents, on September 23, 2026, Craig Yazzie, 35, Angel Smith, 22, and Manualito Begay, 18, all enrolled members of the Navajo Nation, allegedly entered a residence in Nageezi, New Mexico, and assaulted a man with a sledgehammer and dumbbells, leaving him with life-threatening injuries.

Afterward, Yazzie and Smith encountered a family member nearby, and Yazzie allegedly told him they had beaten the victim and left him outside. The family member found the victim beneath a wooden structure near the residence, bleeding from his face and struggling to breathe. 

The victim was airlifted to a local hospital, where medical personnel determined that he had suffered a collapsed lung, a head laceration, and multiple contusions. 

Yazzie, Smith, and Begay were located at a residence in Bloomfield, New Mexico the following day and arrested. 

Yazzie, Smith, and Begay are charged with assault with a dangerous weapon and assault resulting in serious bodily injury. They will remain in custody pending a detention hearing, which has not been scheduled. If convicted of the current charge, the defendants face up to 10 years in prison. 

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Nation Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Eliot Neal is prosecuting the case.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
teaser: Craig Yazzie, Angel Smith, and Manualito Begay are facing federal charges for allegedly beating a man with a sledgehammer and dumbbells, leaving him with life-threatening injuries.
title: Three Men Federally Charged in Brutal Assault That Left Victim with Life-Threatening Injuries

body:
ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock man pleaded guilty in federal court to second-degree murder for the 2025 killing of a woman on the Navajo Nation.

According to court documents, on November 15, 2025, Harlan Joe, 21, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, unlawfully killed Jane Doe at a residence in Shiprock, New Mexico, after a day of drinking. Joe admitted that he punched, kicked, and dragged Jane Doe on the ground and asphyxiated her, causing her death. When officers arrived at the residence, they found Jane Doe deceased outside the house with obvious signs of abuse and trauma and immediately detained Joe. During a subsequent interview, Joe stated that he knew what he was doing and that it was wrong.

Joe pleaded guilty to second degree murder and faces any number of years and up to life in prison at sentencing. 

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office, made the announcement today.

The Farmington Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and the Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Aaron O. Jordan is prosecuting the case.
teaser: Harlan Joe pleaded guilty in federal court to second-degree murder for the 2025 killing of a woman on the Navajo Nation.
title: Shiprock Man Pleads Guilty to Second-Degree Murder
